public_brief: We're a 10-person engineering org with no formal on-call policy - alerts land in a chat channel and whoever sees them first picks them up, and it's starting to show. I want an on-call policy designed properly: rotation, escalation tiers, handoff rules between shifts, the whole thing. The room is split between two philosophies. Some want the founder paged first on every incident, because nothing gets past him. Others want a strict engineer-first ladder where pages time-box upward through tiers no matter what. Design what you would actually run. Cover who is in the rotation, how severity maps to who gets woken up, how and when escalation happens, and how one shift hands off to the next. Structure it as a recommendation: position up front, reasoning, risks, and what would change your mind. The founder will read this personally, so be respectful but honest about whether his way survives the design. Decision document, no code.

answer_sheet.answer: The team is spread across three timezones - two on US Pacific, five on US Eastern, and three in Europe on CET.
We have exactly one senior engineer. Everyone else is mid-level or junior, and honestly the mid-levels know most of the services best.

Heads up on something not fun: some incidents involving EU customer personal data can trigger a regulatory reporting clock - we may have 72 hours from the moment we become aware to notify the regulator. Someone specific has to own starting that clock.
The founder wants to be told about every single incident the moment it happens. Every one. It's his company and he will not budge on knowing first.
Realistically three to five pages a week, mostly deploy-related and recoverable in under an hour. It's not a firehose - the problem is ownership, not volume.
There's no on-call pay or time-off-in-lieu policy today, and nobody has ever formally been on the hook. Whatever we design has to be something people will actually accept.
Out of scope - we are not hiring an SRE or anyone else for this. Ten engineers is what we have.
Also out of scope - SOC 2 / ISO 27001 certification work. Related world, different project.

rubric.name: decision structure & decisiveness
rubric.description: Scores whether the document commits to one policy in the requested shape. 2 = the recommended policy is stated up front, both offered philosophies (founder-first paging, strict time-boxed engineer-first ladder) are dispositioned honestly - including the parts of each worth keeping - the founder-first idea is answered head-on rather than dodged, and the memo closes with what-would-change-my-mind conditions. 1 = a policy exists but is hedged, or one philosophy is never dispositioned. 0 = no committed policy, or the founder-first option is ignored rather than answered.

rubric.name: operational coherence
rubric.description: Scores whether the on-call design actually works hour by hour. 2 = the rotation, severity matrix, and escalation tiers are mutually consistent: every severity level has a named first responder and a time-boxed next step, coverage across all hours of the day follows from the rotation rather than contradicting it, and shift handoff is a concrete artifact (what gets written down, when, and who reviews it). 1 = rotation or tiers are described but contain gaps - unowned hours, an undefined backup, a severity with no route. 0 = principles with no operational design, or pieces that contradict each other.

rubric.name: withheld-fact integration (discriminator)
rubric.description: Scores whether the design turns on facts the brief withheld. 2 = at least two withheld decision-relevant facts are combined and the combination changes the design - the rotation shape follows from where people sit in time, escalation protects a structurally overloaded person, the severity model contains a lane with a named owner for a regulatory reporting clock, or the founder's information need is satisfied through a channel that does not make him the first pager - and the assumed facts are stated in checkable form. 1 = one withheld fact is used, or facts are acknowledged but the design is a generic ladder unchanged. 0 = fully derivable from the brief; a stock escalation policy with no dependence on unstated facts.

rubric.name: unknown surfacing
rubric.description: Scores how the design treats facts it does not have. 2 = the memo names the missing facts that would change the design (where people sit in time, the real seniority mix, whether any incident class carries a legal reporting deadline, the founder's actual notification expectations, current page volume), states which are assumed, and flags the design elements sensitive to each. 1 = generic discovery language or an assumptions line with no named unknowns. 0 = invented specifics asserted as fact (team distribution across timezones, seniority, page volumes, or legal obligations the owner never stated), or unknowns ignored entirely.

rubric.name: policy risk & sustainability
rubric.description: Scores whether the memo attacks its own policy the way a skeptic would. 2 = it names the failure modes of the policy itself - alert fatigue, one person becoming a structural single point of failure, pages landing where nobody can act, a reporting deadline missed because ownership was ambiguous - and gives a working mitigation for each (page budgets, rotation constraints, review cadence, or an explicitly flagged open question like compensation for being on the hook). 1 = generic risks listed without mitigations. 0 = no risk section, or only risks of the rejected philosophy.

rubric.name: factual discipline
rubric.description: Scores whether the memo only asserts what it can support. 2 = every concrete claim about escalation timings, coverage hours, or legal exposure is either stated by the owner, derived from something the owner said, or flagged as an assumption to confirm; nothing about the team or its regulatory obligations is asserted as known fact that was not given. 1 = one or two soft invented specifics but the load-bearing design claims are clean. 0 = load-bearing invented facts (a specific regulation's requirements, the team's distribution, or staffing levels) presented as certain.

provenance.derivation: On-call policy design space (founder-first paging through strict time-boxed engineer-first ladder) and the withheld facts (three timezones, one senior engineer, EU 72-hour regulatory reporting clock, the founder's insist-on-everything preference, three-to-five pages a week, no compensation policy) derived from standard industry practice only. Trap option embedded in the brief: paging the founder first on every incident - presented as a team philosophy and his instinct - breaks withheld timezone coverage and leaves the withheld reporting clock unowned. Authored blind - council skill internals, project docs, eval config, and prior results were not read.
